With edge 5 absent, edge 3 is one of few routes to the output, so deleting it risks disconnecting or starving the output node.
Without the direct input-to-node-2 edge, node 2 carries weaker (or zero) features, so a conv on node 2 -> 3 contributes less.
Activating node 1 with a conv creates new paths through edges 2 and 4, a bigger gain than replacing an existing op on edge 0.
Replacing a 3x3 conv with a parameter-free skip loses capacity, while replacing none or pooling with skip adds or improves a path.
Swapping a 3x3 conv for average pooling discards the most valuable op type, hurting more than replacing none, skip or 1x1 conv.
If edge 0 is none, node 1 receives no input, so a conv on node 1 -> 3 processes zeros and has little effect.
When node 2 has no edge to the output, removing its input edge barely changes the network, so the usual loss from deleting a conv is smaller.
Adding the input-to-output residual where none existed is a large gain, whereas replacing an existing conv on edge 3 trades away capacity.
With no direct input-to-output edge, the output relies on fewer paths, so a strong conv on node 1 -> 3 adds more relative value.

raw:
These ten hypotheses come from structural reasoning about the cell DAG and known NAS-Bench-201 regularities. The planned experiments have no results yet, so none of them are tested.

- **Dead-path effects.** An edit on an edge whose endpoint node has no input or no output barely changes the network.
- **Disconnection.** Removing the last path to the output is catastrophic.
- **Adding versus replacing.** Adding an op where the edge was `none` helps more than overwriting a useful conv or skip.
- **Path scarcity.** Capacity added on a path to the output helps more when the cell has few other such paths.
